thesis.problem: A grid built on wind and solar needs something firm underneath it that is not gas, and the candidates are few. Fission carries a waste and siting problem Germany has already legislated its way out of; fusion has spent seventy years being thirty years away. What changed is that the US National Ignition Facility got more energy out of a laser-driven fusion target than went into it, which turned the question from whether the physics works into whether anyone can build a machine that does it several times a second, commercially.
thesis.solution: Focused Energy pursues inertial confinement: banks of extremely powerful lasers compress a fuel pellet until it fuses, repeated at a rate that makes a power station rather than an experiment. It is a spinout of the Technical University of Darmstadt, it bought two of the world's most powerful existing lasers rather than waiting to build them, and it plans its first laser fusion plant on the site of the decommissioned Biblis nuclear station in Hesse by the mid-2030s.

Secondary write-ups outside the allowlist put it “close to one billion dollars”, which if accurate would be *below* the threshold and would keep the company out; that is why this entry stayed excluded until an allowlisted publication said otherwise. Handelsblatt and TechCrunch both cover the round without a valuation; Gründerszene reports the same round as the moment the company passed a billion — “knackte die Milliarden-Bewertung” — without saying what the figure was. thesis.problem: Europe can build satellites and cannot reliably launch them. Ariane 6 is sized for large payloads on a national cadence, Soyuz stopped being available in 2022, and the small and medium satellites that make up most of what Europe now wants in orbit — earth observation, connectivity, and increasingly sovereign defence capacity — have had to buy rides from American providers on American schedules and American terms.
thesis.solution: Isar Aerospace builds Spectrum, a two-stage rocket sized for the payloads Europe actually flies rather than the ones a national programme was designed around, and manufactures it itself: engines, tanks and avionics in-house, additive manufacturing rather than a supplier chain across a dozen countries, on the argument that vertical integration is what makes launch cheap and the cadence predictable. It is a spinout of the Technical University of Munich and launches from Andøya in northern Norway.

undisclosed.note: Nobody has published a figure for Isar Aerospace, and the register spent a batch establishing that rather than assuming it. Its own release on the €270m Series D was opened and read end to end — round, investors, factory, headcount, no valuation anywhere — and Sifted's account of the same round states none either. The €2bn widely attached to the company traces to a Bloomberg piece whose own URL slug is “isar-aerospace-in-talks-to-raise-250-million-ahead-of-launch”: talks, about a smaller round that was superseded, and all three Wayback captures of that URL are themselves HTTP 403 block pages. What is stated plainly, by an allowlisted publication, is the status and the month: TechCrunch, listing Europe's new unicorns of 2025. That sentence carries no numeral, which is exactly why this record exists in this shape.

The crossing, and an unusual one: the instrument that carried Isar Aerospace over the threshold was a convertible bond rather than a priced equity round, so there is no post-money to disclose and nobody has disclosed one. TechCrunch states the fact and the month in the same sentence as the instrument, which is what this record rests on. Note that the company's own university says the same thing — TUM's press release is titled “Isar Aerospace becomes a unicorn” — but a university announcing its spinout is not on the register's allowlist, so it is mentioned here and not cited.

thesis.problem: Industrial robots are precise and blind. They repeat a taught path inside a safety cage because they cannot perceive what is around them, which means every new task is a re-installation and every task involving a person is a fence. That is workable for a car plant running one model for six years and useless for the labour shortage everyone actually has — the jobs nobody can staff are varied, unstructured and next to people.
thesis.solution: Neura Robotics builds what it calls cognitive robots: arms and humanoids with sensing built into the machine rather than bolted around it, so they can work without a cage and be taught by demonstration instead of programmed. The company designs its own sensors, drives and software stack rather than integrating other people's, and is betting that the same platform serves an industrial arm, a service robot and a humanoid — which is why a robotics company is raising at the scale of an AI one.

disputed.note: Neura itself has never stated a valuation. Its own announcement of this round gives a size and no price, and it declined to comment on the figure. The $7bn reaches an allowlisted page at second hand — Sifted attributes it to the Financial Times “citing people familiar with the deal” — and at third hand in Gründerszene, which prints it flatly as fact in its round-up of 2026's German unicorns: “Die Bewertung: sieben Milliarden Dollar und damit Einhorn-Status.” Two independent allowlisted publications carrying the same number is why it is published here rather than left undisclosed; that neither traces to the company is why it is flagged. A reader should treat the membership as solid and the figure as reported rather than confirmed.

Sifted reports the round flatly as “a $1.4bn Series C round”, which is the figure on file here. The company's own announcement, and Tech.eu reporting it, say “up to $1.4 billion” — a ceiling that unlocks in tranches rather than a sum already wired. thesis.problem: A reconnaissance drone is only useful if the picture it brings back is current, and European armies spent two decades buying small numbers of expensive airframes on procurement cycles measured in years. Its systems flew over 19,000 missions in Ukraine in 2025.

thesis.problem: Deposit rates inside the single market differ by percentage points, and almost nobody can reach them. A saver in Germany is offered whatever their own bank pays; opening an account with a bank in Portugal or Lithuania means a foreign onboarding process, a foreign language and a foreign deposit-guarantee scheme they have no way to assess. The rates exist, the guarantees exist, and the friction between them is what keeps hundreds of billions sitting still.
thesis.solution: Raisin is a marketplace with one onboarding: the saver signs up once and can then place money with any partner bank on the platform across Europe, each covered by its own national deposit guarantee up to the EU-harmonised €100,000. The other half of the business is the mirror image — deposits-as-a-service sold to banks that want funding and to distributors that want a savings product without building one. It brokers tens of billions of euros and has been profitable since 2023.

undisclosed.note: The figure everyone quotes for Raisin is “over two billion euros”, and it is over two billion euros in words rather than digits — Gründerszene spells it out, sourcing it to Finance Forward, and no allowlisted publication has printed it as a numeral. Handelsblatt separately calls the company “milliardenschwer” and nothing more precise. Two further things are worth a reader's attention. This valuation was set by a secondary sale in which existing holders sold shares, not by a priced primary round, so it is a price paid for stock changing hands rather than a post-money — the register publishes those (Trade Republic, n8n) and always labels them. And Raisin's unicorn status has not been continuous: investor Kinnevik marked it at €895m in 2022 and it lost the label, regaining it at the March 2023 upround this record dates the crossing to.

The crossing, and the company is the one that states it. Raisin had been a unicorn once before — Kinnevik marked the merged Raisin DS at €1.3bn in July 2021 — and then was not, after the same investor wrote it down to €895m in 2022. This €60m Series E restored the status, and co-founder Frank Freund says so in the round's own coverage: “Unser Unicorn-Status wurde mit der jetzigen Upround bestätigt.” No figure accompanies it, from the company or from anyone else, which is why the crossing is recorded qualitatively rather than with a post-money.

disputed.note: Not new money into the company: existing holders — Thrive Capital and Christian Angermayer's Apeiron among them, and reportedly the founders in smaller amounts — sold stock to Tencent, Hedosophia and Vitruvian. The amount on file is the “mehr als 100 Millionen Euro” the reporting states and is therefore a floor rather than the sum, which is why it is flagged approximate. The valuation this transaction set is the one carried on the record above, in words rather than digits.

thesis.problem: A great many small businesses sell one good product on Amazon and stall there, because the owner is also the buyer, the marketer and the logistics department. Individually they are too small to negotiate with factories or to fund the next product line; sold individually, they fetch a small-business price.
thesis.solution: Razor Group buys those sellers outright and runs them on shared systems for sourcing, pricing, advertising and supply chain, so the combined group has the volume to bargain with manufacturers and the data to decide what to make next. Growth has come as much from absorbing rival aggregators — Stryze, then the American company Perch — as from buying merchants.

disputed.note: A larger figure is widely attached to Razor: TechCrunch’s headline on the March 2024 Perch merger calls $1.7bn a valuation. Its article body measures something else — “the combined business has an enterprise value of $1.7 billion … with about $400 million of debt on its books”. Enterprise value counts that debt; a post-money equity valuation does not, and the post-money is what this register records. The $1.2bn here is Razor’s last stated post-money, struck at the April 2023 Series C — and still standing a year later, when TechCrunch wrote at the merger that “Razor’s last valuation, when it raised money about a year ago, was $1.2 billion.”

thesis.problem: European road freight is a market of very large shippers and very small hauliers: a manufacturer with thousands of loads a week on one side, and on the other tens of thousands of carriers running a handful of trucks each. Matching them has historically been done by phone and fax through forwarders, and roughly a fifth of trucks run empty because nobody can see the whole board at once.
thesis.solution: sennder is a digital forwarder: it contracts directly with the large shippers and dispatches the work across a connected fleet of third-party carriers through its own platform, so pricing, tracking and settlement are software rather than phone calls. It has grown as much by absorbing rivals — Everoad, Uber Freight’s European arm, C.H. Robinson’s European surface transport business — as organically.

thesis.problem: European defence procurement was built to buy small numbers of expensive platforms over decades. The war in Ukraine showed that attritable strike drones are consumed in thousands per month, and that the bottleneck is not designing one but manufacturing, iterating and fielding them faster than an adversary can adapt their countermeasures.
thesis.solution: Stark builds loitering munitions — drones that hold over an area, find a target and destroy it on impact — and treats production rate as the product. Its stated use of the 2026 round is new electronic-warfare research facilities and scaling output to thousands of systems a month, which is the number that matters in a war of attrition rather than a unit-cost comparison against a missile.

disputed.note: This is the round that crossed the threshold and it was never announced, so the register is publishing the least-disclosed figure in it. What supports the date and the numeral is Sifted, in June 2026, reporting its own earlier finding: the company “reached unicorn status in an unannounced January funding round valuing it at more than $1bn”. When Sifted first reported it in February, the size of the round was undisclosed, the source was Manager Magazin, and the valuation was confirmed only by “a person close to the company”, who put it in a different currency: “Stark is worth more than one billion.” Hence a round here with no amount and no investors — those were never published — and hence this note. A reader should weigh it accordingly: this is the crossing as an allowlisted publication states it, not as the company has ever confirmed it.

thesis.problem: Millions of employees in Germany, Italy and Spain are owed a tax refund and never claim it, because the return assumes vocabulary and paperwork most people do not have. The alternatives are a tax adviser whose fee can exceed the refund, or desktop software that still expects the user to know which boxes apply to them.
thesis.solution: Taxfix replaces the form with a guided set of plain-language questions, selecting only the ones that fit the answers already given, and files the return for a flat fee once the refund is shown. The company is deliberately aimed at simple tax situations — salaried people with a payslip — rather than at the complex cases advisers are built for.

thesis.problem: Retail investing in Europe was priced and packaged for people who already had money. Bank brokerage carried per-order commissions and custody fees large enough to make small, regular savings uneconomic, which left most Europeans dependent on state pensions they are unlikely to be able to live on.
thesis.solution: Trade Republic is a mobile broker with a full German banking licence: commission-free savings plans, fractional shares and ETFs, plus bonds, derivatives and crypto, with a flat external settlement fee instead of a percentage. It earns on order flow, interest on customer deposits and card interchange rather than trading commissions, and now operates across most of western Europe.
